segments.text: IHL regulates the conduct of hostilities and protects persons who are not, or are no longer, taking part in armed conflict.

The core questions are: what type of armed conflict exists, who is protected, what targets may be attacked, and what weapons or methods are restricted. Distinction, proportionality and precautions are central operational ideas.
Primary international authorities: Geneva Conventions and customary IHL as reflected in the ICRC IHL databases.

International humanitarian law applies because an armed conflict exists, not because the conflict has been legally justified under the law on the use of force. This distinction is essential. Jus ad bellum addresses whether resort to force is lawful; jus in bello or IHL regulates conduct once the legal threshold of armed conflict is reached.

The first analytical step is classification. International armed conflicts generally involve resort to armed force between states. Non-international armed conflicts involve sufficiently intense protracted armed violence between state authorities and organized armed groups, or between such groups, subject to the applicable legal tests. Classification determines which treaty rules apply, though customary IHL also matters.

The Geneva Conventions establish protection for wounded and sick members of armed forces, wounded, sick and shipwrecked persons at sea, prisoners of war, and civilians in international armed conflict. Common Article 3 provides minimum protections in non-international armed conflict. Additional treaty and customary rules regulate detention, humane treatment and specific vulnerable categories.

A person may be protected because of status or because the person is hors de combat—out of the fight due to surrender, detention, unconsciousness or another legally recognized condition. Protection is not a reward for political sympathy; it is a legal consequence of humanitarian rules.

Distinction requires parties to direct operations against military objectives and not civilians or civilian objects as such. Proportionality prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Precautions require feasible steps to verify targets and reduce civilian harm.

These principles are connected but different. A civilian object does not become targetable merely because anticipated collateral damage appears small; targetability first depends on whether it qualifies as a military objective. Proportionality is assessed only after a lawful military objective has been identified.

rows: Before and during resort to force

items.text: IHL begins once the legal threshold of armed conflict is met. Its application does not depend on whether one side had a lawful reason to start the conflict.
First classify the conflict as international or non-international because classification affects the applicable treaty framework and legal rules.

The principle of distinction requires parties to distinguish military objectives and combatants from civilians and civilian objects. Proportionality restricts attacks expected to cause excessive incidental civilian harm in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated.

Precautions require feasible steps to reduce civilian harm. Separate rules protect wounded, sick, shipwrecked persons, prisoners and detainees, and persons who are no longer participating in hostilities.
IHL also limits weapons and methods of warfare through treaty and customary rules. Humanitarian protection and military necessity operate within a legal framework, not as unlimited competing slogans.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not confuse IHL with the UN Charter rules on whether force may be initiated. IHL regulates conduct during armed conflict.

items.text: Keep IHL separate from the legality of starting a war.
Prepare protected categories and basic targeting principles.

segments.text: IHL applies because an armed conflict exists, regardless of political justification for it.
Civilians and civilian objects receive protection against direct attack.
Wounded, sick and detained persons have specific protections.
